source: Jaeggi, Buschkuehl, Jonides, Perrig (2008) Improving fluid intelligence with training on working memory
finding: Founding claim. Healthy young adults trained on an adaptive dual n-back task (spatial squares plus spoken letters) and gained on Gf matrix tests more than no-training controls. The gain grew with the number of training days.
numbers: Four experiments (8, 12, 17, 19 sessions; n=16, 22, 16, 15 per experiment). Trained group gain d=0.65 (t(33)=5.53); controls d=0.25 from retest (t(34)=2.08). Group x session F(1,67)=5.27, p<.05, partial eta2=0.07.
limits: No active control. Passive no-contact controls only. Gf measured by one test per experiment (RAPM for 8 days, BOMAT for 12, 17, 19 days). Different tests per dose level.
agent_relevance: Original source of the idea that practicing a general cognitive process lifts reasoning. Our agent has no such route; this is the claim later work failed to confirm.

source: Jaeggi et al. (2008) dose-response result
finding: Gain in Gf rose with training time. The authors read this as a dose-dependent effect and rejected a pure retest account.
numbers: Gain by training time (8, 12, 17, 19 days): F(3,30)=9.25, p<.001, partial eta2=0.48. Post hoc: 8 vs 17 days p<.01; 8 vs 19 days p<.001; 12 vs 19 days p<.01; 12 vs 17 days p=.06. Training gain on the n-back task fit a linear function, R2 0.73 to 0.81.
quote: it is possible to improve Gf without practicing the testing tasks themselves
limits: Dose groups were different people, different samples and different Gf tests (RAPM versus BOMAT), so dose is confounded with test and cohort.
agent_relevance: Dose-response was the strongest argument for causality. If an agent scaffold claims that more rehearsal means better reasoning, ask for the same dose test with an active control.

source: Jaeggi et al. (2008) theory of why transfer should happen
finding: Theory: dual n-back loads executive processes (inhibition, monitoring, dual-task management, updating, binding). These are said to overlap with the processes that Gf tests need. The authors say WM span capacity may not be what changes. They suggest non-capacity skills such as multiple-task management.
numbers: Prior work cited: Raven solving relates to holding many goals in WM (Carpenter, Just, Shell 1990). Transfer to Gf was found even though trained and test tasks look different.
limits: Mechanism is speculative and not tested. Transfer to complex span (WM capacity) was not shown, which weakens the claim that WM capacity itself changed (see Shipstead et al. 2012).
agent_relevance: Useful model of what a transfer claim needs: a named shared process. For a scaffold, check which operator (O1 to O8 in SCHEMA) shares a process with the target task.

source: Jaeggi, Studer-Luethi, Buschkuehl, Su, Jonides, Perrig (2010) The relationship between n-back performance and matrix reasoning
finding: Study 1: single and dual n-back scores correlate about equally with Gf tests and less with an operation span task. Study 2: four weeks of single or dual n-back training gave more Gf gain than no-contact controls. The authors call this a replication and extension.
numbers: Study 1 N=104 (mean age 21.3). Study 2 N=99 Taiwanese undergraduates: 52 controls, 47 training (single n-back about 21 and dual n-back about 25 per group in the tables).
limits: Same lab as the original. No active control, only no-contact. Effect sizes per group were not recovered cleanly from the PDF text.
agent_relevance: Weak support for the claim that n-back relates to Gf more than to span. Links to the factor-structure-of-abilities subfield (parallel note, not covered here).

source: Chooi and Thompson (2012) Working memory training does not improve intelligence in healthy young adults
finding: A direct replication with passive and active control groups and two doses found no improvement in fluid intelligence or WM capacity after dual n-back training, although trained task scores rose.
numbers: N=93 completed. Three groups (passive control, active control, dual n-back) crossed with 8-day or 20-day training; cell sizes ran from n=4 to n=21. Tests: Raven APM (36 items, timed), complex span (OSPAN), Primary Mental Abilities battery. No significant group by time effects and no significant RAPM improvement.
limits: Small cells (as low as 4). Timed Raven with restriction of range in a student sample. Authors criticise Jaeggi 2008 for short, timed, split tests.
agent_relevance: A clean failed replication with an active control. Retest gain in controls is a warning for any agent benchmark: repeated items inflate scores.

source: Redick et al. (2013) No evidence of intelligence improvement after working memory training: a randomized, placebo-controlled study
finding: Young adults got 20 sessions of adaptive dual n-back, or adaptive visual search (placebo), or nothing. Both trained groups improved on their own task. No transfer to any ability test (fluid intelligence, multitasking, WM capacity, crystallized, perceptual speed).
numbers: 20 training sessions; pre, mid and post tests; multiple measures per construct; abstract states high statistical power. Exact N not read.
limits: Abstract read through Europe PMC only; full text not opened. N and effect sizes not recorded here.
agent_relevance: Best-designed single null result: active placebo plus several measures per construct. A model for how to evaluate a scaffold gain.

source: Thompson et al. (2013) Failure of working memory training to enhance cognition or intelligence
finding: Young adults had 20 sessions of adaptive n-back training. They improved on trained tasks, with gains lasting at least 6 months, but showed no transfer to untrained WM tasks, fluid intelligence or other cognition.
numbers: 20 sessions. N not read (full text download failed).
limits: Known only from a search summary of the abstract. Not opened.
agent_relevance: Persistent trained-task gain without transfer: the skill is real but narrow.

source: Sprenger et al. (2013) Training working memory: Limits of transfer
finding: Two experiments trained adults on WM tasks. Gains appeared on the trained task and on tasks that shared stimuli or task features, but no general improvement in WM. Bayes factors favoured the null for general cognitive ability. Controls for need for cognition, beliefs about intelligence and age did not change this.
numbers: Total N=253 over two experiments. Experiment 1: 20 hours over 6 weeks on a battery of adaptive tasks, 127 started and 115 analysed, with a 3-month follow-up. Experiment 2: 264 started, 138 completed, 89 selected for analysis, with an active control and broad versus narrow training arms.
limits: Moderate sample per arm. Arms differ in breadth of training so dose and breadth mix.
agent_relevance: Transfer follows shared stimuli and task features (near transfer). Same rule for scaffolds: gains appear where the format matches.

source: Kuepper and Karbach (2015) Increased training complexity reduces the effectiveness of brief working memory training
finding: Five short sessions of single or dual n-back against a passive control. Neither group improved matrix reasoning. Both lowered general task-switch costs. Only single n-back gave near transfer to an untrained updating task; the simpler training worked better.
numbers: Five sessions of about 30 minutes; passive control. Far transfer to specific switch costs, Stroop and matrix reasoning: none.
limits: Brief training cannot test the 17 to 20 session dose reported by Jaeggi. Passive control only.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: more complex practice can cut transfer. Heavier scaffold steps may not give more benefit.

source: Shipstead, Redick, Engle (2012) Is working memory training effective?
finding: Critical review. Four design problems: single tasks used to define change, invalid WM tasks, no-contact control groups, subjective outcomes. It says the field must show that WM capacity itself rises across varied tasks, and that intelligence gains cannot be readily attributed to WM capacity change.
numbers: Review, no new N. Quotes the optimism of the day (Klingberg 2010; Sternberg 2008; Jaeggi et al. 2011; Morrison and Chein 2011).
quote: there is a need to directly demonstrate that WM capacity increases in response to training
limits: Written before the largest meta-analyses. Authors say they do not aim to settle whether training works.
agent_relevance: Gives the design checklist (active control, many tasks per construct, objective outcomes) to apply when we test a scaffold against plain prompting.

source: Melby-Lervag and Hulme (2013) Is working memory training effective? A meta-analytic review
finding: First big meta-analysis. Training gave short-term gains on WM tasks. Verbal WM gains vanished at follow-up. No convincing generalisation to nonverbal ability, verbal ability, inhibition, decoding or arithmetic.
numbers: 23 studies, 30 group comparisons. As quoted in Soveri et al. (2017): verbal WM g=0.17 (active control) and 0.12 (passive); visuospatial WM g=0.24 (active) and 0.52 (passive); nonverbal problem solving g=0.15 (active) and 0.26 (passive).
limits: Abstract (Europe PMC) plus the numbers quoted by Soveri et al. The original text was not opened.
agent_relevance: The active-versus-passive control gap (0.15 vs 0.26) is the pattern to look for in any scaffold comparison.

source: Melby-Lervag, Redick, Hulme (2016) Working memory training does not improve performance on measures of intelligence or other measures of far transfer
finding: Updated meta-analysis. Reliable gains on intermediate transfer (verbal and visuospatial WM) right after training. No convincing far-transfer gains when WM training is compared with a treated control. The size of the WM gain did not predict far-transfer size. Publication bias analysis: no evidential value in the treated-control studies.
numbers: 87 publications, 145 experimental comparisons. A 2019 reanalysis of the learning-disability subsample reported far transfer g=0.02 and near transfer g=0.37 (via search summary).
quote: no convincing evidence of any reliable improvements when working memory training was compared with a treated control condition
limits: Abstract read only (full text sites were blocked). Exact far-transfer g values not recorded.
agent_relevance: Strongest summary of the negative result. The mediation test (WM gain does not explain far transfer) fits the idea that an intermediate cause does not carry over.

source: Au et al. (2015) Improving fluid intelligence with training on working memory: a meta-analysis
finding: Meta-analysis of n-back studies with Gf outcomes in healthy adults aged 18 to 50. Found a small positive transfer to Gf and several moderators.
numbers: 20 studies. Gf g=0.24 overall as cited by Soveri et al. 2017; Au et al. 2016 later reported g=0.13 (as quoted by Soveri).
limits: Only the abstract and numbers quoted by Soveri were read. Active-control effects are smaller than passive.
agent_relevance: The most optimistic meta-analysis still gives a small effect that shrinks with better controls.

source: Soveri, Antfolk, Karlsson, Salo, Laine (2017) Working memory training revisited: A multi-level meta-analysis of n-back training studies
finding: Multilevel meta-analysis of n-back training. Large effect on the trained n-back task, small on other WM, small on cognitive control and Gf. Effects did not depend on training dose, single versus dual n-back, or age.
numbers: 284 effect-size values verified. By domain: n-back g=0.62 [0.44, 0.81]; WM g=0.24 [0.16, 0.32]; cognitive control g=0.16 [0.05, 0.27]; Gf g=0.16 [0.08, 0.24]. In the control analysis: overall g=0.11 [0.00, 0.22], p=.048; n-back g=0.59; WM g=0.18; cognitive control g=0.08 (p=.202); Gf g=0.11 (p>.05). Age effect QM(1)=0.07, p=.794.
limits: Pooled effects mix passive and active controls. Authors note outliers. The Gf effect becomes non-significant in the pretest-controlled analysis.
agent_relevance: Even for the original n-back method, far transfer to Gf is about 0.1 SD after control. Our agent should not plan on practice-driven reasoning gains.

source: Sala and Gobet (2017) Does far transfer exist? Negative evidence from chess, music and working memory training
finding: Summary of meta-analyses. For WM training the overall effect on other abilities is small and shrinks as design quality rises. Active-control comparisons are near zero.
numbers: WM training overall g=0.12 [0.06, 0.18]; fluid intelligence 0.11 [-0.02, 0.24]; cognitive control 0.09 [-0.08, 0.26]; mathematics 0.20 [0.03, 0.36]; literacy 0.11 [0.00, 0.22]. Passive control 0.18 (k=34); active control 0.05 [-0.05, 0.15] (k=40). Near transfer 0.44 (active) and 0.46 (passive).
quote: the optimism about far-transfer effects of cognitive training is not justified
limits: Pooled estimate is mainly children and young adolescents. Authors suggest placebo and expectation as the cause of far-transfer gains.
agent_relevance: The active-versus-passive gap (0.18 vs 0.05) is the quantitative case for always using an active control when we measure scaffold gains.

source: Gobet and Sala (2022) review of cognitive training far transfer (second-order data from Sala et al. 2019)
finding: Second-order meta-analysis. For WM training the far-transfer effect is about 0.12 uncorrected and about 0.00 when publication bias is removed and only active controls are used.
numbers: Uncorrected: typically developing children g=0.13 (k=25); children with learning disabilities 0.12 (k=18); adults 0.12 (k=44); older adults 0.13 (k=32). Corrected, active only: 0.01 (k=15), 0.02 (k=12), 0.00 (k=27), 0.01 (k=16). Heterogeneity tau2=0. Placebo effects roughly 0.15 to 0.20 SD at best. Grand mean across 14 first-order meta-analyses: 0.12, then 0.00.
quote: the likelihood that cognitive training provides broad cognitive and academic benefits is very low indeed
limits: Authors argue the null view. Only the first 100,000 of 147,000 characters of the page were read.
agent_relevance: tau2=0 means no moderator matters: there is no subgroup where WM training reliably transfers. This closes the shortcut route.

source: Simons et al. (2016) Do brain-training programs work?
finding: Large review in Psychological Science in the Public Interest. Found no compelling evidence that computerised brain training gives broad cognitive benefits or real-world gains beyond the practiced tasks.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Known from a press summary in search results. Not opened.
agent_relevance: Consensus statement of the field; supports the negative-result framing.

source: Hu and Lewis (2025) Do Language Models Understand the Cognitive Tasks Given to Them? Investigations with the N-Back Paradigm
finding: Re-tests the claim by Gong et al. (2024) that GPT-3.5 has a working memory capacity limit of about 3. Poor 2- and 3-back scores come at least partly from failing to understand and keep the task. Weak models act as if doing an m-back with m not equal to n.
numbers: Retrieval accuracy on 1-, 2-, 3-back (24-letter sequences): Qwen 1.5 14B 1.00/0.09/0.08; Llama 3.1 8B 1.00/0.14/0.17; Gemma 2 27B 1.00/0.57/0.36; GPT-3.5 Turbo 1.00/0.51/0.43; Qwen 2 72B 1.00/0.81/0.84; Llama 3.1 70B 1.00/0.99/0.93. Llama 3.1 70B at 8, 9, 10-back: exact retrieval 75.25%, 66.08%, 57.1%; task accuracy 83.33%, 78.25%, 71.92%. With a demonstration curriculum: 90.08%, 90.08%, 84.75%.
limits: All stimuli sit in the context window, so the task tests attention lookup, not a human-like store. Open models plus GPT-3.5 only.
agent_relevance: N-back is a prompt-following test for LLMs, not a capacity test. A curriculum of demonstration sequences (1-back up to n-back) raised accuracy at large n: in-context practice, not weight training.

source: Gong et al. (2024) n-back with GPT-3.5 (as described by Hu and Lewis 2025)
finding: First n-back study on an LLM. Reported that GPT-3.5 accuracy fell from 1-back to 3-back and concluded a working-memory capacity limit of about 3, similar to humans.
numbers: Dataset reused by Hu and Lewis: 24-letter sequences. GPT-3.5 Turbo retrieval accuracy 1.00/0.51/0.43 for 1/2/3-back in the reanalysis.
limits: Original paper not opened; second-hand from Hu and Lewis (2025).
agent_relevance: Warns against reading human-style capacity into LLM scores.

source: Huang, Sun, Wang, Dredze (2025) Language Models Do Not Have Human-Like Working Memory
finding: Argues that n-back and other in-context tasks let LLMs read answers from the context. Introduces three tasks that need latent state held without writing it out: Number Guessing, Yes-No Deduction, Math Magic. Seventeen frontier models from four families show irrational or self-contradicting behaviour.
numbers: Number Guessing: the sum of Yes probabilities over numbers 1 to 10 should be 1 if a number is held. GPT-4o-2024-08-06 gave 1.085; DeepSeek-R1 0.640; several models 0. Yes-No Deduction (200 trials): GPT-4o had 173 failures (passed 27); GPT-4o-Mini failed in all 200 in the first setting. Math Magic: chain of thought and reasoning models raised accuracy; DeepSeek-R1 100%; the number seven made up 66.7% (o1-mini), 46.9% (o3-mini) and 68.5% (o4-mini) of correct answers.
limits: Tasks designed by the authors; no human baseline in the pages read. Reading of results as lack of working memory is theirs.
agent_relevance: Supports our design: write intermediate state into the text (chain of thought, scratch state) instead of relying on latent memory. Externalising helps; there is no memory to train.

source: Liang, Zhu, Wang, Zhou (2026) Can Vision Replace Text in Working Memory? Evidence from Spatial n-Back in Vision-Language Models
finding: Qwen2.5 and Qwen2.5-VL on a spatial n-back with matched text or image grids. Text gave higher accuracy and d-prime than vision. Log-probability analysis shows nominal 2- and 3-back often follows a recency-locked comparison, not the instructed lag.
numbers: Table 1 (accuracy, 200 random grids; condition columns not fully recoverable): Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct text 80.50, 73.00, 62.00, 55.00; Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct text 70.00, 63.50, 58.00, 53.50; Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct vision 78.50, 82.00, 77.00, 80.50.
limits: Small 7B models. Column labels in the extracted table were not fully clear.
agent_relevance: Same lesson as Hu and Lewis: n-back scores can hide recency shortcuts. If we use n-back as a probe, check the lag.

source: Search for LLM studies that train working memory to raise reasoning (none found)
finding: Searches (search engine, arXiv) returned LLM n-back and working-memory benchmarks, not studies of WM-training transfer in LLMs. The nearest analogue is in-context demonstration curricula (Hu and Lewis).
numbers: 0 LLM WM-training transfer studies found; 3 LLM WM-probe papers found (Hu and Lewis 2025; Huang et al. 2025; Liang et al. 2026).
limits: Absence after a limited search; Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex were rate limited. Not proof that none exist.
agent_relevance: The negative result carries over: no training-style shortcut. Our scaffold must work at inference time.

source: Backward digit span as an LLM working-memory benchmark (search result, details unread)
finding: A paper proposes backward digit span to measure the working part of working memory in LLMs. The search summary says performance correlates with Raven's Progressive Matrices and ARC-AGI-1.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Only the search summary was seen. Not opened; verify before citing.
agent_relevance: If true, a WM probe tracks reasoning scores across models. That is a correlation between models, not training transfer.

source: Soveri et al. (2017) Table 1: earlier WM-training meta-analyses as printed
finding: Across earlier meta-analyses, near-transfer WM effects exceed Gf effects, and Gf effects are small and fall when active controls are used.
numbers: Examples printed in the table: Gf g=0.24 (Au 2015); Gf g=0.15 (active, nonverbal) vs 0.26 (passive, nonverbal) with verbal 0.04 and 0.02; Gf g=0.05 (active) vs 0.20 (passive); WM near transfer g between 0.17 and 0.79 depending on study and control.
limits: Columns were merged in the PDF extraction, so figures may be assigned to the wrong meta-analysis.
agent_relevance: Pattern: trained task large, near WM moderate, Gf small, and Gf shrinks with active controls.

source: Hu and Lewis (2025) mechanism analysis: retrieval log-probabilities and m-back confusion
finding: Log-probability analysis: under 2-back instructions, weak models (tier T3) still give most probability to 1-back continuations, and demonstrations do not offset the strong 1-back prior. For the best model, the retrieval probability peaks at m=n and falls off symmetrically as m moves away from n, which the authors read as true n-back understanding.
numbers: Tiers by 2-/3-back accuracy: T1 above 80%; T2 about 50% on 2-back and 40% on 3-back; T3 about 20%. Models: Llama 3.1 70B (T1), Gemma 2 27B (T2), Qwen 1.5 14B (T3). Gemma 2 27B with interactive demos: 0.61 (+.04) on 2-back and 0.31 (-.05) on 3-back.
limits: Interpretive; depends on the prompt format of Gong et al. Qwen 1.5 14B marked N/A on some demo conditions.
agent_relevance: A model's score on a cognitive task can be a prior about the task, not a capacity. Test whether our scaffold changes the task the model thinks it is doing before crediting it with a skill gain.
